Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here for millions of players who own a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X / S, and those who plan to buy a console, despite rising costs this year, just to play it. As you have likely already noticed, the launch is inescapable, and that’s especially tough if you’re a PC gamer.

I’m sorry to remind you that the clock has only just now started ticking down to the unannounced yet inevitable release of the PC version. Good luck with avoiding Twitch and browsing the internet while trying to remain oblivious to the violent (and romantic) delights that await you.

According to recent reports, seeing Leonida in true 4K at an unlocked frame rate with full ray-tracing effects and extended draw distances, among other graphical improvements, might be a thing you can do on your PC as early as sometime in Q1 2027, if recent reports are accurate. Regardless, early 2027 is not right now. Speaking as someone with a capable gaming desktop, I’m sad to say that FOMO has already gotten the best of me. I bought GTA VI on the PS5 and will probably double-dip and buy it again on PC, just like I did with GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2. The psychology of me, a weak-willed consumer, is one that publisher Rockstar Games and really any other organization in its position would be happy to exploit.

The PC version of GTA VI will launch, eventually, in a very different landscape than the PC ports of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA V did. Despite the recent downturn in PC sales driven by increased RAM prices, there are considerably more players on PC now than there were a decade ago. SteamDB’s charts show that Steam’s concurrent users alone have more than doubled (from around 20 million to over 40 million now) since 2020.

A chunk of those people are likely made up of console expats who decided to migrate to PC for various reasons. Some wanted to experience the fun of building their own desktop, while some were mainly convinced by the fact that you can get more power for your money with a PC than with a PlayStation 5 Pro or Xbox Series X. For a subset of people, the convenience of getting something like a Steam Deck to bring your PC game library with you anywhere more than makes up for its lack of power. There are many other justifiable reasons for making PC your main gaming platform, like getting faster access to discounts on digital games, not paying for online multiplayer, ultrawide monitor resolutions, being able to buy games from one of several platforms, and having one device that you can use for work and play.

Industry observers note that rockstar seems poised to deliver the definitive version of GTA VI on PC on its own terms, and I’m interested to see what the end result will be. In addition to building the best-looking version of the game made to run well across countless configurations, its PC optimization efforts are likely also more focused than before on ensuring decent performance on lower-end hardware (including PC handhelds). With a 200-plus-gigabyte install size on consoles, I dread how major it’ll be on PC.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, the PC version will launch alongside an improved version of GTA Online (whether it’s free to play is anyone’s guess), and maybe with upgraded GTA roleplay tech to support it. I’m hopeful that the PC version of GTA VI will come in early 2027, but if the numerous delays of the console versions were any indication, the developer will take all the time it needs to get it right.

Update, 9:55AM ET, November 19th: The SteamDB data cited now specifies that it’s concurrent consumers, not the number of users total.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nintendo’s classic SNES console now has its own ChatGPT chatbot.
  • AI runs on GPUs, so I wondered: how good would @ChatGPT be if it ran on the Super NES's best GPU, the Super FX 2 chip?
  • The above Tweet shows you the SNES app splash screen, chat window, and an animation of someone interacting with chat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nintendo’s classic SNES console now has its own ChatGPT chatbot. Due to the platform's age and limited resources, things are kept in check, though. For example, the (small) language model is a 2.2-million-parameter distillation of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b. Nevertheless, Vintage Computing blogger Benj Edwards has attempted to squeeze the best performance from this incongruous tech combo by accelerating the chatbot's responsiveness using “the Super NES's best GPU, the Super FX 2 chip.”.

AI runs on GPUs, so I wondered: how good would @ChatGPT be if it ran on the Super NES's best GPU, the Super FX 2 chip? With the help of GPT-6 Astra and gpt-oss, I present unofficial ChatGPT for SNES: 2.2M parameters on a real Super Nintendo. It can make mistakes, but it's fun https://t.co/TAJ4jYREo7November 19, 2026.

The above Tweet shows you the SNES app splash screen, chat window, and an animation of someone interacting with chat. If that’s tempting you to give ChatGPT for SNES a test run, there are several options. Easiest first, you can head on over to this page where Edwards has embedded the SNES9x emulator, which can load the app. Once there, choose the 4MB model, or a 19MB one with the opening sentences of 150,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles integrated into the knowledge base (stored in the cartridge's MSU-1 data file). We recommend the latter, so the model knows a few more facts and can work as a calculator.

When you load it, the SNES app asks you to press Start. If you are sat at your PC keyboard, just hit Enter. You don’t need a joypad for text entry either, thankfully; just get typing to interact with ChatGPT for SNES (as long as the window is in focus). While you’re interacting with this chatbot, you can enjoy SNES-appropriate input sound effects, plus a chirpy chip-tune soundtrack.

In our tests, the usefulness of the ChatGPT for SNES app, beyond its curiosity value, was very limited. Edwards admits as much on the project's embedded interactive page, explaining that “the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT.” Naturally, with a small and fuzzy knowledge base, “You’ll get some fun and weird stuff,” says the Vintage Computing blogger.

Using Nintendo Super FX 2 technology to accelerate the language model is a masterstroke for the project. This coprocessor chip enhanced SNES games with faster 2D and 3D graphics and debuted with Yoshi's Island. Inside the SFX2, which had to be manufacturer-installed on any game cartridge that required it, was a 21.47 MHz RISC CPU. Contrast that to the SNES main CPU, a 16-bit Ricoh 5A22 running at 2.68 MHz.

Nintendo's second version of the SFX retained the polygon and advanced 2D effect capabilities of the original but ran at full speed internally (rather than half speed) and supported larger ROM sizes. Like Yoshi’s Island, it would be integrated into the Doom cartridge.

Industry observers note that edwards’ ChatGPT for SNES isn’t just an online diversion. It can also be downloaded and run/played on a real vintage SNES. You’ll also need a flash cart for the console with Super FX support, and MSU-1 support if you prefer the build including the abridged Wikipedia fact book.

In a recent development, the ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your people discover first: broken layouts, usability challenges that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that introduces the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Recent findings suggest that even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:.

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce newly introduced violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

In a recent development, there are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

It has been revealed that these platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

In a recent development, chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

According to recent reports, pricing: Free initiative with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and customers. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

In a recent development, trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so proposal coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

According to recent reports, strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free proposal includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited customers and projects.

Industry observers note that trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs promptly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Industry observers note that applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

According to recent reports, strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with massive cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

According to recent reports, backstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Sources indicate that strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report indicates reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Recent findings suggest that trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

According to recent reports, playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an patch flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that demonstrates the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Industry observers note that visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Industry observers note that visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a newly introduced framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:.

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change highlights up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:.

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

According to recent reports, playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

It has been revealed that UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Recent findings suggest that playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

Valve declared some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

Rapidus reportedly struggles to produce working SRAM on its 2nm node, putting 2027 mass production at risk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rapidus is reportedly facing challenges in developing functioning SRAM cells using its 2nm-class node, which relies on EUV lithography.
  • In a recent development, bloomberg's report spells bad news for the Japanese firm.
  • "Then we had a testing and July 10th we confirmed a major milestone: we successfully obtained electrical characteristics of 2-nanometer node GAA transistors," stated Atsuyoshi Koikem, chief executive of Rapidus, at Hot Chips 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rapidus is reportedly facing challenges in developing functioning SRAM cells using its 2nm-class node, which relies on EUV lithography. According to a fresh report, Rapidus has missed a critical milestone to demonstrate working SRAM cells this summer, despite the Japanese tech giant's efforts in producing semiconductor test structures at its fab in Japan in mid-2025. In addition, the company is allegedly fighting contamination in its cleanroom. This puts the prepares of the government-backed startup to begin mass production of chips in 2027 at risk.

In a recent development, bloomberg's report spells bad news for the Japanese firm. Rapidus began to produce test structures with 2nm-class Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors at its IIM-1 facility in Hokkaido in July 2025, nearly 16 months ago. At the time, the organization declared that its prototype transistors exhibited the expected electrical characteristics, which suggested that its equipment and fundamental process steps worked as intended.

"Then we had a testing and July 10th we confirmed a major milestone: we successfully obtained electrical characteristics of 2-nanometer node GAA transistors," stated Atsuyoshi Koikem, chief executive of Rapidus, at Hot Chips 2025. "We can see the transistor actually works.".

Recent findings suggest that however, production of individual transistors is considerably easier than fabrication of functional integrated circuits (ICs) with multiple interconnected devices. According to sources at Bloomberg, Rapidus was supposed to demonstrate functional static random-access memory (SRAM) cells by summer 2026, but has yet to achieve this milestone. It is noteworthy that the report does not reveal whether Rapidus is struggling with individual SRAM cells, larger memory arrays, or achieving acceptable electrical characteristics and yields, so we will have to speculate.

SRAM is fundamental to modern processors because it serves as cache memory and forms other on-chip memory structures, which can contain hundreds of millions of bitcells. Furthermore, SRAM arrays are important vehicles for early process evaluation, as their repetitive structures expose manufacturing defects, transistor variability, and other problems that may not become apparent during tests of individual transistors.

Recent findings suggest that A conventional 6T SRAM bitcell consists of six transistors: two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) and two access transistors. However, these transistors also require contacts and local interconnects, as well as connections to wordlines, bitlines, and power rails (VDD and VSS). Meanwhile, a complete SRAM macro also requires peripheral circuits, such as row decoders, sense amplifiers, write drivers, and control logic, which makes a 256 KB SRAM macro quite a sophisticated IC. As a result, chipmakers usually use both SRAM cell arrays and SRAM macros as primary means to evaluate, monitor, and qualify process technologies at various stages. Furthermore, low defect density of SRAM macros is crucial for good yields of SRAM-intensive chip designs.

Industry observers note that the importance of SRAM makes Rapidus' reported difficulties particularly concerning given its intention to begin commercial production in 2027. While the company does not confirm delays in mass production using its 2nm fabrication technology, in an interview with the Japan Times, representatives at Rapidus already said that the company was on track to mass-produce chips in the second half of fiscal 2027, which ends on March 31, 2028. Previously, Rapidus had specified its production targets without specifying calendar years or fiscal years, which by default implied the calendar year.

Before it can mass-produce processors for customers, the company must demonstrate functional SRAM cells, integrate them into larger arrays, achieve acceptable yields, qualify its process technology, and then initiate risk production around a year before the start of high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

Chipmakers do not generally disclose detailed schedules for SRAM development and milestones as far as upcoming manufacturing technologies are concerned. However, TSMC tends to share progress on its upcoming nodes using the performance and yield of a 256 Mb SRAM array or '256 Mb SRAM yield on an internal product-like vehicle.' For example, TSMC's N2 demonstrated more than 80% of its target device performance and over 50% yield on a 256Mb SRAM test chip in April 2023. By April 2024, the process had advanced to more than 90% of its target device performance and over 80% SRAM yield. About half a year before mass production started, in May 2025, N2 transistor performance was close to 100%, whereas 256 Mb SRAM average yield was over 90%. By contrast, Rapidus has not revealed any SRAM progress so far, and Bloomberg reports that the organization has failed to produce functioning static random access memory cells, meaning that its SRAM yield is 0%.

While there is no rule of thumb that a manufacturer must have a functional SRAM array or macro N quarters before mass production of chips with that array or macro, it is evident that the reported setback leaves Rapidus with limited time to complete its crucial development milestones before kicking off mass production by the end of fiscal 2027.

Production of 2nm-class chips with GAA transistors and extreme ultraviolet lithography is exceptionally complicated, even for established chipmakers. So far, only Intel, TSMC, and Samsung have begun mass production of chips using nodes that rely on GAA devices. Unlike FinFETs, GAA transistors feature multiple vertically stacked silicon nanosheets surrounded by gate materials, which improves electrostatic control but introduces additional fabrication challenges. Furthermore, extremely small feature dimensions require exceptional precision in deposition, etching, lithography, and process control. For Rapidus, which was founded only in 2022 and relies on process technology IP developed by IBM, the task of reproducing these processes consistently in a new fab represents an incredibly tall task.

One potential problem involves selective removal of silicon-germanium (SiGe) layers that separate silicon nanosheets during fabrication. These sacrificial layers must be removed without damage to the silicon channels or significant changes to their dimensions. Insufficient etching can leave unwanted material between nanosheets, whereas excessive etching can reduce channel thickness or increase surface roughness. A research paper published by imec identifies nanosheet release as one of the critical challenges of GAA manufacturing, particularly because variations in channel geometry can affect transistor performance and consistency.

It has been revealed that in fact, EUV lithography itself introduces additional complications. At extremely small dimensions, stochastic effects associated with photon absorption, resist chemistry, and subsequent pattern transfer can produce variations in feature dimensions, edge roughness, and occasional missing or malformed structures. Such defects can affect pretty much everything, including transistor gates, contacts, and interconnects. In fact, there is a firm called Fractilia that specializes solely in stochastic controls. Although individual test transistors may function correctly, circuits with millions of interconnected devices are much more vulnerable to failures caused by stochastic defects.

In a recent development, another potential challenge concerns inner spacer formation. These extremely small dielectric structures electrically isolate the gate from the source and drain regions. Their fabrication requires precise lateral etching of SiGe followed by dielectric deposition. Variations in spacer geometry can affect effective gate length, parasitic capacitance, leakage current, and transistor performance. A paper published in Nanomaterials in January 2026 demonstrates that even subtle differences in etching conditions can affect spacer geometry and nanosheet integrity, which potentially introduces electrical variability that becomes particularly problematic in SRAM circuits.

It has been revealed that gate stack integration presents another possible source of difficulties. GAA fabrication requires conformal deposition of gate dielectrics and metal materials around multiple nanosheets, including narrow spaces between them. Variations in material thickness, interfaces, and effective metal work function can alter transistor threshold voltages, which is not a big problem for individual transistors or tiny test patterns. However, for SRAM structures, excessive differences between nominally identical transistors can reduce read, write, and retention margins, which could prevent cells from operating reliably at their intended voltages and greatly narrow the manufacturing process window.

Sources indicate that finally, contact resistance, interconnect defects, and particle contamination can further complicate circuit integration. Bloomberg specifically reports that Rapidus is working to improve dust and particle control in its cleanroom. Normally, there might be no connection between contamination and the SRAM woes the company is experiencing. However, one of the distinct features of IIM-1 is that it uses an unconventional grid-based wafer transportation system to enable its single-batch processing as well as increase the efficiency of expedited processing. Usage of this system raises questions about whether the fresh infrastructure has undergone sufficient contamination and reliability qualification, though, again, a transportation system alone could not be responsible for zero (or near-zero) SRAM yield.

Rapidus reportedly stresses that it remains committed to mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027. However, until the manufacturer demonstrates functional SRAM and subsequently larger integrated circuits, questions about its ability to manufacture commercially viable 2nm chips will persist.

According to recent reports, anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.

It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”.

Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the major story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.

Industry observers note that so drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money.
  • Recent findings suggest that start with the local preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production complications that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:.

Recent findings suggest that start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

In a recent development, 1. Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

It has been revealed that 2. Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

Sources indicate that 3. Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

According to recent reports, set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

In a recent development, the peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:.

Sources indicate that 1. Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2. Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

Sources indicate that 3. When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

Industry observers note that 4. For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

It has been revealed that 5. On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:.

Industry observers note that 1. Create a latest RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

Industry observers note that 2. Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

Sources indicate that 3. In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4. In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

Industry observers note that one peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1. The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2. The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3. The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

Sources indicate that 4. Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

Recent findings suggest that on a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Recent findings suggest that consumers deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try fresh network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

It has been revealed that mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

It has been revealed that 1. Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

Industry observers note that 2. In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3. Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

Sources indicate that 4. Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

According to recent reports, 5. Check the negotiated codec and how promptly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Sources indicate that once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals demonstrates the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Industry observers note that start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that experimental PC modder Trash Bench recently tested a laptop cooler and tried to beat it with increasingly powerful blower setups, eventually opting for a bounce house inflator blower to cool the i7-10750H and RTX 2070 MaxQ with a 90W power limit. He was able to bring temperatures down from 84 degrees Celsius to 48.8 degrees Celsius, with Cyberpunk going from 47 FPS to 56 FPS.

Trash Bench was asked to review a laptop cooling stand, but he stated he doesn’t do reviews, so he proposed a video idea: He’ll test the laptop cooler and try to beat it with his creations—no opening the laptop, no sub-ambient cooling solutions, only airflow.

Industry observers note that the Llano V12 laptop cooling fan sent to Trash Bench achieved an impressive 58.3 degrees Celsius average on the GPU at medium settings, dropping 27 degrees from the stock 84 degrees Celsius. The lower temperatures also improved gaming performance by an average of 19.4%. Pushing the Llano V12 to 100% made it incredibly loud, but it only reached 56.7 degrees Celsius with negligible performance gains.

It has been revealed that his first attempt to beat the Llano V12 was using the Noctua NF-A20, a huge 200mm fan, and a 3D-printed duct with foam around the edges, like the Llano V12, to prevent air leaks. Unfortunately, the single 200mm fan didn't beat the Llano V12, with GPU temperatures averaging 66.3 degrees Celsius—still pretty impressive given the setup's simplicity, if you ignore the messy PC power supply and fan speed controller beside it.

Industry observers note that his second attempt used six Arctic P12 fans at full speed, beating the Llano V12 by 0.9 degrees Celsius at medium settings and achieving an average GPU temperature of 57.4 degrees Celsius. However, it lost to the full-speed Llano V12, but only barely. The third attempt used two 4000 RPM server fans, which were even louder than the six full-speed Arctic P12S — but that finally did the trick, beating the Llano V12 at 100% by 2.6 degrees Celsius.

In a recent development, and just to go extreme, like Trash Bench often does in his experiments, he used a powerful blower fan designed to inflate bounce houses. He took advantage of the larger foam gaskets the Llano V12 used and 3D-printed an interface at the bottom of the laptop cooler’s housing to fit a flexible duct. The sheer force of the air lifted the laptop off the stand, so it needed to be taped down to seal the air leak.

Sources indicate that the bounce house blower produced an average GPU temperature of 48.8 degrees Celsius, but saw very little performance gain over the Llano V12 at 100%, six Arctic P12s, and the pair of server fans, with Time Spy benchmark results within 1% of each other. The Noctua was the weakest in the benchmarks, however, lagging by 3% behind the bounce house blower, but was much quieter.

Trash Bench admits that while lower temperatures are great, they reach diminishing returns once the thermal bottleneck disappears and another bottleneck takes over.

Google Fi app redesign brings floating toolbar & Ask Fi

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.
  • It has been revealed that previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar.
  • The tabs remain Home, Plan, Billing, Shop, and Support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

It has been revealed that previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching update declared last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

The tabs remain Home, Plan, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space.

There’s now a floating action button for the new Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over.

Sources indicate that this redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side update. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the newly introduced first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

It has been revealed that secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • First up, our resident CPU boffin, Jake Roach, has been on the show floor all week, offering us a direct line to all the goings-on at the conference, including an interesting back-and-forth from Nvidia and AMD on their CPUs.
  • In this interview, we sit down with Finder to find out how Vera came to be, what agentic workloads mean for the CPU industry, and where Nvidia's headed next.
  • It has been revealed that nvidia's Vera CPU was a hot topic at SC26, as the company explained that existing software cannot always take full advantage of the processor without architecture-specific optimization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First up, our resident CPU boffin, Jake Roach, has been on the show floor all week, offering us a direct line to all the goings-on at the conference, including an interesting back-and-forth from Nvidia and AMD on their CPUs. AMD claims that its latest EPYC Venice lineup is the best at agentic workloads, while Nvidia's marketing material characterized Nvidia's Vera CPU as being purpose-built for Agentic AI. At SC26, Nvidia CPU chief Ian Finder rebuked Nvidia's own marketing material, stating that the idea that Nvidia could have predicted the Data Center moment was "absurd," instead saying that the manufacturer's design know-how helped them develop the processor.

In this interview, we sit down with Finder to find out how Vera came to be, what agentic workloads mean for the CPU industry, and where Nvidia's headed next.

It has been revealed that nvidia's Vera CPU was a hot topic at SC26, as the company explained that existing software cannot always take full advantage of the processor without architecture-specific optimization. The company revealed that under some workloads, Vera's performance can be optimized by up to 39% when taking its Olympus-based Arm cores into account. However, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained from Olympus-specific hardware optimization workloads other than matrix multiplication.

Nvidia also unveiled a Rubin GPU variant, named Rubin HPC, a chip that the company claims is purpose-built for agentic workflows and scientific simulations that demand processing large datasets. While technical details remain scant, Nvidia says that Rubin HPC sports over 50,000 CUDA cores, or slightly below double the number of cores present in the standard-issue Rubin GPU. We explored all the details and possibilities that the newly announced chip might offer.

AMD is now featured in over 40% of the new TOP500 list of supercomputers, with a 14% boost to the company's position. Leading the company is Lux, a supercomputer developed in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Energy. The second supercomputer, Discovery, is expected to debut in 2028, sporting a suite of EPYC CPUs and Instinct accelerators.

It has been revealed that within the TOP500, not much has changed... at the top, with the top 10 systems remaining unchanged, as China's LineShine system in Shenzhen remains at the top of the list, with El Capitan remaining second. We take a look at the entire list and how the focus has seemingly shifted toward AI compute capacity. While the demand for HPC hardware is at an all-time high, it appears as though the vast majority of that hardware isn't being tested against the TOP500 benchmark.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, despite AI clusters seemingly eating up compute capacity, AMD recognizes that the burgeoning segment will never wholly replace HPC computing, and that high-precision workloads will continue to be necessary. AMD's Scott Tease further suggested that building a heterogeneous compute stack would be the best path forward for tackling complex research problems. This point dovetails nicely into how AMD additionally touted that its MI430X's native FP64 operations will beat out emulated support for the full-precision data types seen in Nvidia's hardware. This is notable, as the company claims that Ozaki FP64 emulation could have cascading effects on memory usage, which is in notorious levels of undersupply.

Not wanting to be left out of the conversation, Intel's next-generation Diamond Rapids CPUs surfaced at SC26, but not from Intel itself, curiously. On the ground, we saw the chips turn up at the CXL booth and at Bull, where the CPU was shown installed in a server. While there were no demos available, the organization did show off demos for Xeon 6+ and its Crescent Island GPU.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere at the show, PCI 6 devices and controllers have started to surface. First, Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was demoed at the show, armed with PerformaShape 2, which increases the number of quality-of-service sets from 256 to 512, alongside additional boons.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, Phison detailed two latest enterprise SSDs: one that comes with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory, and another that is set to merge pSLC cache, with high QLC capacity on a single controller. We explore what makes these devices notable and why, though the tech giant itself notes that the devices are very much still in development.

VAST Data explained how petabyte-scale SSDs will outgrow the tried and true RAID parallel filesystems, according to a simulation the manufacturer ran on its own 900 PB system, which puts the odds of data loss at a staggering 1 in 11 over a decade. We explain all in detail about how it works.

Industry observers note that as enterprise hardware and the titanic growth of AI superclusters push the limits of our existing material infrastructure, from interconnects to grid energy and raw materials, researchers from The Ohio State University discussed how high-performance networking could soon scale across entire regions. We explore how faster networking connections could spell a future where distributed computing systems communicate across vast distances.

While we have a few more articles waiting to be published from SC26, we've also been hard at work publishing stories from other corners of the industry. To read these, you'll need to first arm yourself with a Tom's Hardware Premium subscription.

Recent findings suggest that this week, Anthropic debuted on the NYSE, but the frontier AI lab's debut is also colored by the backdrop of what seems like an endless barrage of upcoming vulnerabilities, hacks, and AI-powered action by would-be malfeasants. The conversation around AI safety, sparked by OpenAI's HuggingFace incident, is also being used as a Trojan horse for safety legislation, and against this backdrop, we explore how the companies shaping AI safety might also be the ones warning against using competitors, like capable Chinese open-weight AI models.

Anthropic has also been busy bringing up more compute resources, notably publishing how it managed to get its Claude Mythos model to optimize its software stack to work with AMD Instinct hardware in around three days, with little human oversight. What once was a relentless task that took significant man-hours, an AI can now help complete in mere days. Such a feat could endanger Nvidia's highly lucrative CUDA moat, as AI continues to transform the hardware landscape.

It has been revealed that intel's acquisition of Quantum computing company Classiq is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, and following it, Intel is poised to have a chance at becoming the first full-stack quantum computing vendor. The company also plans to manufacture quantum processors on its 18A process, offer foundry services, and eventually sell quantum computers.

In a recent development, an unmanned chip fab might be an unthinkable future today, but it's a future that chipmakers are already planning for. SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron, known rivals in the memory industry, have formed a body to standardize robotic charging, with the aim of having robots from different manufacturers share equipment and therefore cut the costs and complexity of deploying fleets of robotic workers.

Email remains an key communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep users informed.

For developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

Sources indicate that SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

In a recent development, for example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:.

The application detects an event.

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The provider processes the request.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:.

In a recent development, this example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

Industry observers note that this is an notable security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

According to recent reports, not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

Its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:.

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The important consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

This is where webhooks become useful.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:.

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and update the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:.

This is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

It should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:.

The backend stores the new user.

A verification email is triggered.

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:.

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

Recent findings suggest that automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

DomainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Sources indicate that domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

In a recent development, email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

It has been revealed that for example, open tracking can be affected by privacy features and automated image loading. Click tracking may also include automated security scans.

More reliable application-level signals can include:.

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Sources indicate that developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery concerns without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

When collecting engagement information, applications should follow applicable privacy requirements and respect user communication preferences.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:.

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an notable part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

It has been revealed that REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and update their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

  • “They’re making so much money they don’t know what to do with it,” the U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump, who has been pushing for AI development in the U.S., stated that he wants to prevent U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries or charge them with a “tremendous tax” if they push ahead with their overseas prepares. The move comes as a surprise, Trump said, as he hasn’t even discussed the proposed policy with his cabinet and advisors, reports Axios.

“They’re making so much money they don’t know what to do with it,” the U.S. president remarked. He added that Americans should negotiate with AI hyperscalers that want to establish data centers in communities, as they could help reduce costs and taxes. “They have plenty of money. Take it,” Trump added.

Several states and jurisdictions have started implementing similar solutions, with one Pennsylvania town listing 43 specific demands to approve an AI data center, while Fresh York State recommended the municipalities demand a $1 million community investment per megawatt. Some developers embraced this, with one offering $10,000 per household if its 1,3000-acre facility gets approved, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX is buying out 418 homes near its flagship AI data center.

Industry observers note that this is going to be an problem for many Americans, though, especially as AI data center measures put forward in the recently concluded mid-term elections have been comprehensively defeated. In fact, data center moratoriums have already surged past 500 across the U.S., making it harder for developers to push forward with their projects.

One possible reason Trump is considering a ban on overseas data centers for U.S. companies is that Chinese AI labs have been exploiting a loophole in U.S. law. This technicality has allowed them to export data to overseas data centers that use AI chips banned for export to China, like Nvidia’s Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips. “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” Trump mentioned.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) in January 2026 to close the workaround, but the bill has been in limbo in the Senate since then. The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is also taking steps to prevent this, with Nvidia warning its clients that their customers should be at least 51% not from China to avoid legal exposure.

Another question is how the Trump administration will implement its “tremendous tax.” Congress is the only federal body with the constitutional power to impose taxes, and with the opposing party controlling both the House and the Senate, it would be doubly hard for the White House to implement its legislative priorities without serious concessions.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that finally, there’s the issue of data sovereignty and latency. U.S. companies would build data centers in foreign countries because some governments demand that their data remain within their territory. So, if Washington proceeds with the ban, American tech companies could potentially lose this market. Aside from that, keeping data centers in the U.S. would result in longer latency and slower responses, making it harder to serve customers located on the other side of the globe.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Canva today announced “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.
  • Recent findings suggest that generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today announced “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

Recent findings suggest that generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

For some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

According to recent reports, to give its owners the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

Put simply, this is great to see.

AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

In a recent development, for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Recent findings suggest that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

Industry observers note that an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

According to recent reports, proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

Industry observers note that when you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Industry observers note that pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

In addition, with a wrap-around glass side panel and triple-chamber design, the case comes with three Corsair RS-R 120mm PWM ARGB fans, which normally run $60 on their own.

According to recent reports, typical of these multi-chamber case designs, the AIR 5400 RS-R supports most hardware you can throw at it. You can use anything from a mini ITX motherboard to an E-ATX board, and it has mounting points for up to two 360mm radiators, plus an additional 120mm mounting point. The 360mm worth of mounting space on the bottom of the case is occupied by the pre-installed fans and an airflow shroud.

According to recent reports, additionally, the case is compatible with rear-connector motherboards from Asus, MSI, and Gigabyte, so you can have a cable-free front chamber. The case doesn't have a vertical GPU mount, but there's ample room for even larger graphics cards, with a maximum length of 430 mm supported. Like most multi-chamber cases, this one is primarily designed around liquid cooling. However, you have a generous 180mm of CPU cooler clearance if you decide to go with an air cooler.

Industry observers note that the Corsair AIR 5400 RS-R is a midtower PC case with three Corsair RS-R 120mm ARGB fans pre-installed. It supports up to E-ATX motherboards, as well as rear-connector boards from MSI, Asus, and Gigabyte.

Sources indicate that the Corsair AIR 1500 RS-R is loaded with enough features to justify its $250 list price, let alone its current sale price of $170. In addition to wide cooling and GPU compatibility, along with rear-connector motherboard support, the case comes with a built-in anti-sag arm to support your GPU, the height of which you can adjust depending on your GPU. Be warned, however, that the final fan on especially long GPUs may hit the support. Thankfully, you can remove it.

Recent findings suggest that corsair includes its RapidRoute 2.0 mounting system, giving you a pegboard-style motherboard tray that provides mounting points virtually anywhere for cable management. Cable managing multi-chamber cases is much easier than a traditional tower, as well, with ample room behind the motherboard tray to hide your cable mess.

Around the front, the curved-glass side panel shows off the internals of your rig from the side and front. To get inside, the curved panel splits apart like French doors, so you can service your machine without juggling a few different pieces of tempered glass. The rear side panel is on a hinge for easy access, as well.

The one major downside with this chassis is that it doesn't come with any front panel USB-A ports. Instead, you get three USB-C ports, split between two USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports and a single Gen 2 port, alongside a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack. Given that most motherboards have one or maybe two USB-C ports, extra front panel connectors are always nice to have. However, even a single USB-A would go a long way.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.
